items.readable_text:
Content:
When a Fourier series represents a function [MATH: f], it is often much easier to differentiate the series term-by-term than to recompute a brand-new Fourier series from scratch.

Content:
However, term-by-term differentiation is only guaranteed to work when the underlying periodic function is sufficiently "well-behaved".

Content:
The theorem about term-by-term differentiation of Fourier series states the following:

Content:
> Suppose that
> [MATH: f(x) \sim \dfrac{a_0}{2} + \sum_{n=1}^{\infty} a_n\cos\bigg(\dfrac{n\pi}{L}x\bigg)+b_n\sin\bigg(\dfrac{n\pi}{L}x\bigg)]
> is a [MATH: 2L]-periodic function which is
>
> - piecewise smooth, and
> - continuous.
>
> Then, the Fourier series of [MATH: f'(x)] can be obtained by differentiating term-by-term the Fourier series of [MATH: f(x){:}]
> [MATH: f'(x) \sim \sum_{n=1}^{\infty} -\dfrac{n\pi a_n}{L}\sin\bigg(\dfrac{n\pi}{L}x\bigg)+\dfrac{n\pi b_n}{L}\cos\bigg(\dfrac{n\pi}{L}x\bigg)]

Content:
In other words, if [MATH: f(x)] is the [MATH: 2L]-periodic extension of a function [MATH: F(x)] defined on [MATH: x \in [-L,L),] then the Fourier series of [MATH: f'(x)] can be obtained by differentiating term-by-term the Fourier series of [MATH: f(x)] provided that

Content:
- [MATH: F(x)] is continuous on [MATH: x \in (-L,L),]
- [MATH: F(x)] is piecewise smooth on [MATH: x \in (-L,L),] and
- [MATH: \lim\limits_{x \to -L^+} F(x) = \lim\limits_{x \to L^-} F(x).]

Content:
Note: The constant term [MATH: \dfrac{a_0}{2}] disappears after differentiating, since [MATH: \dfrac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}\!\left(\dfrac{a_0}{2}\right)=0.]

Term-by-term differentiation is a huge time-saver: it lets us obtain a Fourier series for [MATH: f'(x)] without recomputing Fourier coefficients from scratch.

Content:
But differentiation also tends to make Fourier series "less convergent", it "spends" one power of [MATH: n]. So, we need to be careful about what the differentiated series actually does.

Content:
In a [MATH: 2L]-periodic Fourier series, differentiating
[MATH: \cos\!\left(\dfrac{n\pi x}{L}\right) \qquad \text{or} \qquad \sin\!\left(\dfrac{n\pi x}{L}\right)]
introduces a factor of [MATH: \dfrac{n\pi}{L}]. So, very roughly,
[MATH: \big(\text{new coefficient size}\big) \approx n \cdot \big(\text{old coefficient size}\big).]
That means one level of coefficient decay is "used up" when we differentiate.

Content:
For example, consider the so-called triangle wave and sawtooth wave, the [MATH: 2\pi]-periodic extensions from [MATH: x \in [-\pi,\pi)] to [MATH: x \in \mathbb{R}] of the functions [MATH: y=|x|] and [MATH: y=x,] respectively.

Content:
Their Fourier series are the following:
[MATH: |x| \sim \dfrac{\pi}{2}-\dfrac{4}{\pi}\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\dfrac{\cos\!\big((2n-1)x\big)}{(2n-1)^2}
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
x \sim 2\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\dfrac{(-1)^{n+1}}{n}\sin(nx)]

Notice that:

Content:
- For the continuous and piecewise smooth triangle wave:

- The function has enough "smoothness" (continuity) that its Fourier coefficients decay quickly at a rate of [MATH: \sim \dfrac{1}{n^2}.]
- Differentiation "costs" one level of decay:
[MATH: n \cdot \dfrac{1}{n^2} = \dfrac{1}{n}]
Since the terms [MATH: \dfrac{1}{n}] still approach [MATH: 0,] the series can converge. At the "corners," it settles on the average of the left- and right-hand slopes.

[MATH: n \cdot \dfrac{1}{n} = 1]
Since the terms of the series do not approach [MATH: 0,] the series fails the basic divergence test and does not converge.

Content:
Just like differentiation, integration can also be applied directly to a Fourier series. This is often useful when we already know the Fourier series of [MATH: f(x)] and want a series for an antiderivative of [MATH: f(x)] without recomputing Fourier coefficients from scratch.

Content:
The theorem about term-by-term integration of Fourier series states the following:

Content:
> Suppose that
> [MATH: f(x) \sim \dfrac{a_0}{2} + \sum_{n=1}^{\infty} a_n\cos\bigg(\dfrac{n\pi}{L}x\bigg)+b_n\sin\bigg(\dfrac{n\pi}{L}x\bigg)]
> is a [MATH: 2L]-periodic function which is piecewise continuous. Then, an antiderivative [MATH: F(x)], where [MATH: F'(x) = f(x)], can be found by integrating the Fourier series of [MATH: f(x)] term-by-term:
> [MATH: F(x) \sim \dfrac{a_0}{2}x + C + \sum_{n=1}^{\infty} \bigg( \dfrac{a_n L}{n\pi}\sin\bigg(\dfrac{n\pi}{L}x\bigg)-\dfrac{b_n L}{n\pi}\cos\bigg(\dfrac{n\pi}{L}x\bigg) \bigg)]
> where [MATH: C] is an arbitrary constant of integration.

Content:
Watch out! Note the following caveats:

Content:
1. The expression for the antiderivative [MATH: F(x)] is not a Fourier series in the usual sense because it contains the linear term [MATH: \dfrac{a_0}{2}x.]
2. Even if [MATH: f(x)] is periodic, its antiderivative [MATH: F(x)] is not necessarily periodic. In particular, if [MATH: a_0 \neq 0,] then the term [MATH: \dfrac{a_0}{2}x] grows without bound as [MATH: x] increases.

Content:
If we want a periodic antiderivative, we typically need the average value of [MATH: f] over one period to be [MATH: 0] (equivalently, [MATH: a_0=0]), so that the linear term disappears.

Content:
Note: Integration is generally "safer" than differentiation for Fourier series. Differentiation can slow convergence or even destroy it, whereas integration divides the [MATH: n]th coefficient by [MATH: n,] which typically improves convergence.

lesson.readable_text:
Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:
When a Fourier series represents a function [MATH: f], it is often much easier to differentiate the series term-by-term than to recompute a brand-new Fourier series from scratch.

Content:
However, term-by-term differentiation is only guaranteed to work when the underlying periodic function is sufficiently "well-behaved".

Content:
The theorem about term-by-term differentiation of Fourier series states the following:

Content:
> Suppose that
> [MATH: f(x) \sim \dfrac{a_0}{2} + \sum_{n=1}^{\infty} a_n\cos\bigg(\dfrac{n\pi}{L}x\bigg)+b_n\sin\bigg(\dfrac{n\pi}{L}x\bigg)]
> is a [MATH: 2L]-periodic function which is
>
> - piecewise smooth, and
> - continuous.
>
> Then, the Fourier series of [MATH: f'(x)] can be obtained by differentiating term-by-term the Fourier series of [MATH: f(x){:}]
> [MATH: f'(x) \sim \sum_{n=1}^{\infty} -\dfrac{n\pi a_n}{L}\sin\bigg(\dfrac{n\pi}{L}x\bigg)+\dfrac{n\pi b_n}{L}\cos\bigg(\dfrac{n\pi}{L}x\bigg)]

Content:
In other words, if [MATH: f(x)] is the [MATH: 2L]-periodic extension of a function [MATH: F(x)] defined on [MATH: x \in [-L,L),] then the Fourier series of [MATH: f'(x)] can be obtained by differentiating term-by-term the Fourier series of [MATH: f(x)] provided that

Content:
- [MATH: F(x)] is continuous on [MATH: x \in (-L,L),]
- [MATH: F(x)] is piecewise smooth on [MATH: x \in (-L,L),] and
- [MATH: \lim\limits_{x \to -L^+} F(x) = \lim\limits_{x \to L^-} F(x).]

Content:
Note: The constant term [MATH: \dfrac{a_0}{2}] disappears after differentiating, since [MATH: \dfrac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}\!\left(\dfrac{a_0}{2}\right)=0.]

Content:
In the next slides, we will apply this theorem to a specific example to see how it works in practice.

---

Item 2 — Example: Identifying Properties of Periodic Extensions

Example Prompt:
[MATH: {− 2x,|x ∈ [− 2, 0); x^{2},|x ∈ [0, 2)]
The above function [MATH: F(x)] is defined on [MATH: x \in [-2,2).] Let [MATH: f(x)] be the [MATH: 4]-periodic extension of [MATH: F(x)] to [MATH: x\in\mathbb{R}.]
Determine whether each statement below is true or false.

1. [MATH: F(x)] is continuous on [MATH: x\in(-2,2).]
2. [MATH: F(x)] is piecewise smooth on [MATH: x\in(-2,2).]
3. [MATH: \lim\limits_{x \to -2^+} F(x) = \lim\limits_{x \to 2^-} F(x).]
4. [MATH: f(x)] is piecewise smooth and continuous on [MATH: \mathbb{R}.]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
Let's examine the given statements in turn.

- Statement I is true. The function [MATH: F(x)] is continuous on [MATH: x \in (-2,2).] Its graph is shown below.

[IMG: /graphics/f536c645bf6b1cd0ea1bbc8576eeb69b]

- Statement II is true. The function [MATH: F(x)] is piecewise smooth on [MATH: x \in (-2,2).] It consists of two smooth pieces.
- Statement III is true. Indeed, we have
[MATH: \lim\limits_{x \to -2^+} F(x) = \lim\limits_{x \to -2^+} (-2x) = -2(-2) = 4]
and
[MATH: \lim\limits_{x \to 2^-} F(x) = \lim\limits_{x \to 2^-} x^2 = (2)^2 = 4.]
So, [MATH: \lim\limits_{x \to -2^+} F(x) = \lim\limits_{x \to 2^-} F(x).]
- Statement IV is true since statements I, II, and III are all true.

Note: The [MATH: 4]-periodic extension of [MATH: F(x)] to [MATH: x \in \mathbb{R}] has the graph shown below.

[IMG: /graphics/b3c8ff64307e627d983401287be632ae]

Item 5 — Example: Differentiating a Fourier Series

Example Prompt:
Let [MATH: f(x)] be the [MATH: 10]-periodic extension of the function
[MATH: F(x)=\dfrac{5}{2}x^2-3]
defined on [MATH: [-5,5).] Fill in the blanks in the reasoning below, showing the derivation of the Fourier series of the [MATH: 10]-periodic extension of [MATH: G(x)=5x]
from the corresponding Fourier series of [MATH: f(x).]

> The Fourier series of [MATH: f(x)] is given by
> [MATH: XXXXX]
> Since [MATH: f] is [MATH: XXXXXXXX]
> and [MATH: XXXXXXXX]
> on [MATH: \mathbb{R},] we may differentiate its Fourier series term-by-term to get
> [MATH: XXXXXX]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
First, notice that [MATH: F(x)] is an even function. So, the Fourier series of its [MATH: 2L]-periodic extension has the form
[MATH: \dfrac{a_0}{2} + \sum_{n=1}^\infty a_n \cos\left(\dfrac{n\pi x}{L}\right).]

In our case, [MATH: L=5.] Thus, the Fourier series of [MATH: f(x)] is given by
[MATH: f(x) \sim \dfrac{107}{6}
+ \sum_{n=1}^\infty \dfrac{250(-1)^n}{n^2\pi^2}
\bbox[4pt, border: solid 0.5pt black]{\cos\left(\dfrac{n\pi x}{5}\right)}.]

Now, notice that

- the function [MATH: F] is continuously differentiable on [MATH: (-5,5),]
- continuous on [MATH: [-5,5),] and
- satisfies [MATH: F(-5)=F(5),] if we extend the value at [MATH: x=5] using the formula [MATH: F(x)=\dfrac{5}{2}x^2-3.]

Therefore, the [MATH: 10]-periodic extension [MATH: f] is [MATH: \bbox[4pt, border: solid 0.5pt black]{\text{continuous} }] and [MATH: \bbox[4pt, border: solid 0.5pt black]{\text{piecewise smooth}}]
on [MATH: \mathbb{R},] so we may differentiate its Fourier series term-by-term:

[MATH: (d)/(dx)((5)/(2)x^{2} − 3)|∼(d)/(dx)((107)/(6)) + ∑_(n = 1)^(∞)(d)/(dx)((250(− 1)^{n})/(n^{2}π^{2})\cos ((nπx)/(5))); 5x|∼0 + ∑_(n = 1)^(∞)(250(− 1)^{n})/(n^{2}π^{2}) ⋅ (− (nπ)/(5)\sin ((nπx)/(5))); 5x|∼∑_(n = 1)^(∞)(− 50(− 1)^{n})/(nπ)\sin ((nπx)/(5)); 5x|∼∑_(n = 1)^(∞)50 (− 1) n + 1 n π ⋅ sin ⁡ (n π x 5).]

Item 8 — Tutorial: A Word on Convergence

Content:
Term-by-term differentiation is a huge time-saver: it lets us obtain a Fourier series for [MATH: f'(x)] without recomputing Fourier coefficients from scratch.

Content:
But differentiation also tends to make Fourier series "less convergent", it "spends" one power of [MATH: n]. So, we need to be careful about what the differentiated series actually does.

Content:
In a [MATH: 2L]-periodic Fourier series, differentiating
[MATH: \cos\!\left(\dfrac{n\pi x}{L}\right) \qquad \text{or} \qquad \sin\!\left(\dfrac{n\pi x}{L}\right)]
introduces a factor of [MATH: \dfrac{n\pi}{L}]. So, very roughly,
[MATH: \big(\text{new coefficient size}\big) \approx n \cdot \big(\text{old coefficient size}\big).]
That means one level of coefficient decay is "used up" when we differentiate.

Content:
For example, consider the so-called triangle wave and sawtooth wave, the [MATH: 2\pi]-periodic extensions from [MATH: x \in [-\pi,\pi)] to [MATH: x \in \mathbb{R}] of the functions [MATH: y=|x|] and [MATH: y=x,] respectively.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/f4c92fa6e81d5e7529f60efceb32aa48]

Content:
Their Fourier series are the following:
[MATH: |x| \sim \dfrac{\pi}{2}-\dfrac{4}{\pi}\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\dfrac{\cos\!\big((2n-1)x\big)}{(2n-1)^2}
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
x \sim 2\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\dfrac{(-1)^{n+1}}{n}\sin(nx)]

Content:
The convergence of their corresponding derivatives is summarized in the table below.

Content:
| Function Type | Continuity | Fourier Series Coefficient Decay | Derivative Series Convergence |
| Triangle wave | Continuous | [MATH: O\!\left(\dfrac{1}{n^2}\right)] | Converges / (to the average of slopes) |
| Sawtooth wave | Discontinuous | [MATH: O\!\left(\dfrac{1}{n}\right)] | Diverges |

Content:
Notice that:

Content:
- For the continuous and piecewise smooth triangle wave:

- The function has enough "smoothness" (continuity) that its Fourier coefficients decay quickly at a rate of [MATH: \sim \dfrac{1}{n^2}.]
- Differentiation "costs" one level of decay:
[MATH: n \cdot \dfrac{1}{n^2} = \dfrac{1}{n}]
Since the terms [MATH: \dfrac{1}{n}] still approach [MATH: 0,] the series can converge. At the "corners," it settles on the average of the left- and right-hand slopes.
- For the discontinuous but piecewise smooth sawtooth wave:

- The function's jump discontinuities "use up" the smoothness budget. The coefficients decay only at a rate of [MATH: \sim \dfrac{1}{n}.]
- Differentiation cancels out the decay entirely:
[MATH: n \cdot \dfrac{1}{n} = 1]
Since the terms of the series do not approach [MATH: 0,] the series fails the basic divergence test and does not converge.

Item 9 — Tutorial: Integrating Fourier Series

Content:
Just like differentiation, integration can also be applied directly to a Fourier series. This is often useful when we already know the Fourier series of [MATH: f(x)] and want a series for an antiderivative of [MATH: f(x)] without recomputing Fourier coefficients from scratch.

Content:
The theorem about term-by-term integration of Fourier series states the following:

Content:
> Suppose that
> [MATH: f(x) \sim \dfrac{a_0}{2} + \sum_{n=1}^{\infty} a_n\cos\bigg(\dfrac{n\pi}{L}x\bigg)+b_n\sin\bigg(\dfrac{n\pi}{L}x\bigg)]
> is a [MATH: 2L]-periodic function which is piecewise continuous. Then, an antiderivative [MATH: F(x)], where [MATH: F'(x) = f(x)], can be found by integrating the Fourier series of [MATH: f(x)] term-by-term:
> [MATH: F(x) \sim \dfrac{a_0}{2}x + C + \sum_{n=1}^{\infty} \bigg( \dfrac{a_n L}{n\pi}\sin\bigg(\dfrac{n\pi}{L}x\bigg)-\dfrac{b_n L}{n\pi}\cos\bigg(\dfrac{n\pi}{L}x\bigg) \bigg)]
> where [MATH: C] is an arbitrary constant of integration.

Content:
Watch out! Note the following caveats:

Content:
1. The expression for the antiderivative [MATH: F(x)] is not a Fourier series in the usual sense because it contains the linear term [MATH: \dfrac{a_0}{2}x.]
2. Even if [MATH: f(x)] is periodic, its antiderivative [MATH: F(x)] is not necessarily periodic. In particular, if [MATH: a_0 \neq 0,] then the term [MATH: \dfrac{a_0}{2}x] grows without bound as [MATH: x] increases.

Content:
If we want a periodic antiderivative, we typically need the average value of [MATH: f] over one period to be [MATH: 0] (equivalently, [MATH: a_0=0]), so that the linear term disappears.

Content:
Note: Integration is generally "safer" than differentiation for Fourier series. Differentiation can slow convergence or even destroy it, whereas integration divides the [MATH: n]th coefficient by [MATH: n,] which typically improves convergence.

Content:
Next, let's see a concrete example.

---
